# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

138	
139	The validation review's inventory (owner request, 2026-08-13): every element
140	of the real platform the model does **not** simulate, why, and what defends
141	the design at that boundary. A test here cannot catch a bug living exactly
142	on one of these; anything listed as *assumption* is a place live operation
143	can still teach us.
144	
145	| unmodeled element | what the real world does | what defends the design there |
146	|---|---|---|
147	| **Cron delivery** | `schedule:` is a request to queue: fires land minutes-to-tens-of-minutes late, are silently dropped under load, and GitHub disables schedules after 60 days of repo inactivity ([github-actions-scheduling](../../../packs/git-github/skills/github-actions-scheduling/SKILL.md)) | late/dropped fires ARE modeled abstractly (`dropSchedulerRuns`/`schedulerRunAt` — S4, S5); every rule derives due-ness from durable state, never from "the cron fired"; the 60-day disable is inherited risk, mitigated as today (repo activity from the mechanism's own writes) |
148	| **Actions start latency** | a queued workflow may wait minutes before running; the drain is not really at scheduler run+40s | nothing depends on start latency; all deadlines (leashes, staleness) are hours against minutes of jitter |
149	| **Scheduler run serialization** | two scheduler runs racing is prevented by the workflow `concurrency` group, an Actions feature the sim assumes rather than models | S6 models the *guards* under a duplicated fire; the group is platform config, verified in the migration burst (B1) |
150	| **REST list freshness** | no documented bound on when a list from another node reflects a creation seconds old | **F16**: the scheduler run assumes duplicates WILL happen and self-heals (close all open family items but the oldest) — S30 |
151	| **Label API atomicity** | a swap is two calls; no CAS; either can fail or land alone | labels are visibility + pick filter, never the arbiter — comments arbitrate (§6.2); a torn swap's stateless item is repaired by the janitor's fourth rule; modeled atomically here, defended structurally there |
152	| **Comment ordering** | `created_at` has 1-second granularity (simultaneous claims tie); comment **ids** are server-assigned, strictly increasing | the design orders by id, never timestamp (§6.2); the sim's `seq` models exactly that id order |
153	| **Claim-comment interleaving** | true API interleaving between executors | modeled as stale-snapshot races (`raceExecutorsAt` — S7, S32), which covers the protocol's decision points but not GitHub's own consistency between a comment post and a comment list; residual assumption: a comment list read after posting includes all earlier-id comments |
154	| **Body-edit lost updates** | two concurrent body edits: last write wins, no merge | single-writer-per-state by construction: only the claim winner edits an item's body, and only the scheduler run (serialized by its concurrency group) rewrites the board; residual: a human editing concurrently loses one edit — accepted, the record comments survive |
155	| **Event delivery** | `labeled` webhook events are droppable | modeled only as `eventLost` on creation (S16); every flow is poll-guaranteed by the scheduler run's drain — events are latency sugar everywhere by design |
156	| **Rate limits / quotas** | API quotas, secondary rate limits | costs estimated in DESIGN §5 (hourly-task churn); not modeled; the burst (B-rows) observes real consumption |
157	| **Clocks** | runner clocks skew; only server timestamps are trustworthy | no rule compares runner clocks; ordering is by server-assigned ids, durations by server timestamps; anchors tolerate minute-scale skew by construction (scheduler run-quantized) |
158	| **The invocation wire** | the routine-fire API's real contract, timeouts, the nonce's payload grammar | the *semantics* (at-most-once, the refused/unanswered split, the leash settling the unknown case) are modeled (S9a/S10a/S10b); the wire format is not — burst rows B3/B7 prove it live |
159	| **Actions variable delivery** | `vars.CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL` reaches a run's env only at run start — a value changed mid-run is invisible to it | by design: suspension gates starts, never running work (S37 asserts exactly that boundary); the stamp is stub wiring, burst-verified |
160	| **Workflow concurrency between the scheduler run and a long drain** | the scheduler run and drain share a workflow whose `concurrency` group holds the next cron fire until the whole run ends — a drain doing hours of real work starves the hourly scheduler run | the decoupling wiring (work-as-work review, DESIGN §10): the drain must run outside the scheduler run's serializing group once work may legally outlive an hour; platform config the sim cannot see, verified in the migration burst |
161	| **Secrets & permissions** | Actions secret storage, env stamping, write-gating of labels/comments | prose + conformance checks (§14 secrets path); burst row B4/B7 |
162	| **Search index** | minutes-stale, eventually consistent | never used by the design (F11) — the REST issue list is the only read |
163	| **Real code-work/agent content** | side effects, repos, PRs, sessions | durations and verdicts are scenario inputs; the outcome ceiling and record formats are the engine's existing tested surface |
164	
165	Fidelity grows only when a scenario needs it — an entry leaves this table by
166	becoming modeled, never by being forgotten.

## The unsimulated world

The validation review's inventory (owner request, 2026-08-13): every element
of the real platform the model does **not** simulate, why, and what defends
the design at that boundary. A test here cannot catch a bug living exactly
on one of these; anything listed as *assumption* is a place live operation
can still teach us.

| unmodeled element | what the real world does | what defends the design there |
|---|---|---|
| **Cron delivery** | `schedule:` is a request to queue: fires land minutes-to-tens-of-minutes late, are silently dropped under load, and GitHub disables schedules after 60 days of repo inactivity ([github-actions-scheduling](../../../packs/git-github/skills/github-actions-scheduling/SKILL.md)) | late/dropped fires ARE modeled abstractly (`dropSchedulerRuns`/`schedulerRunAt` — S4, S5); every rule derives due-ness from durable state, never from "the cron fired"; the 60-day disable is inherited risk, mitigated as today (repo activity from the mechanism's own writes) |
| **Actions start latency** | a queued workflow may wait minutes before running; the drain is not really at scheduler run+40s | nothing depends on start latency; all deadlines (leashes, staleness) are hours against minutes of jitter |
| **Scheduler run serialization** | two scheduler runs racing is prevented by the workflow `concurrency` group, an Actions feature the sim assumes rather than models | S6 models the *guards* under a duplicated fire; the group is platform config, verified in the migration burst (B1) |
| **REST list freshness** | no documented bound on when a list from another node reflects a creation seconds old | **F16**: the scheduler run assumes duplicates WILL happen and self-heals (close all open family items but the oldest) — S30 |
| **Label API atomicity** | a swap is two calls; no CAS; either can fail or land alone | labels are visibility + pick filter, never the arbiter — comments arbitrate (§6.2); a torn swap's stateless item is repaired by the janitor's fourth rule; modeled atomically here, defended structurally there |
| **Comment ordering** | `created_at` has 1-second granularity (simultaneous claims tie); comment **ids** are server-assigned, strictly increasing | the design orders by id, never timestamp (§6.2); the sim's `seq` models exactly that id order |
| **Claim-comment interleaving** | true API interleaving between executors | modeled as stale-snapshot races (`raceExecutorsAt` — S7, S32), which covers the protocol's decision points but not GitHub's own consistency between a comment post and a comment list; residual assumption: a comment list read after posting includes all earlier-id comments |
| **Body-edit lost updates** | two concurrent body edits: last write wins, no merge | single-writer-per-state by construction: only the claim winner edits an item's body, and only the scheduler run (serialized by its concurrency group) rewrites the board; residual: a human editing concurrently loses one edit — accepted, the record comments survive |
| **Event delivery** | `labeled` webhook events are droppable | modeled only as `eventLost` on creation (S16); every flow is poll-guaranteed by the scheduler run's drain — events are latency sugar everywhere by design |
| **Rate limits / quotas** | API quotas, secondary rate limits | costs estimated in DESIGN §5 (hourly-task churn); not modeled; the burst (B-rows) observes real consumption |
| **Clocks** | runner clocks skew; only server timestamps are trustworthy | no rule compares runner clocks; ordering is by server-assigned ids, durations by server timestamps; anchors tolerate minute-scale skew by construction (scheduler run-quantized) |
| **The invocation wire** | the routine-fire API's real contract, timeouts, the nonce's payload grammar | the *semantics* (at-most-once, the refused/unanswered split, the leash settling the unknown case) are modeled (S9a/S10a/S10b); the wire format is not — burst rows B3/B7 prove it live |
| **Actions variable delivery** | `vars.CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL` reaches a run's env only at run start — a value changed mid-run is invisible to it | by design: suspension gates starts, never running work (S37 asserts exactly that boundary); the stamp is stub wiring, burst-verified |
| **Workflow concurrency between the scheduler run and a long drain** | the scheduler run and drain share a workflow whose `concurrency` group holds the next cron fire until the whole run ends — a drain doing hours of real work starves the hourly scheduler run | the decoupling wiring (work-as-work review, DESIGN §10): the drain must run outside the scheduler run's serializing group once work may legally outlive an hour; platform config the sim cannot see, verified in the migration burst |
| **Secrets & permissions** | Actions secret storage, env stamping, write-gating of labels/comments | prose + conformance checks (§14 secrets path); burst row B4/B7 |
| **Search index** | minutes-stale, eventually consistent | never used by the design (F11) — the REST issue list is the only read |
| **Real code-work/agent content** | side effects, repos, PRs, sessions | durations and verdicts are scenario inputs; the outcome ceiling and record formats are the engine's existing tested surface |

Fidelity grows only when a scenario needs it — an entry leaves this table by
becoming modeled, never by being forgotten.

900	  baselining runs first, extract and promote follow *the same night* in
901	  order; on the routine night where baselining's precondition declines at
902	  its anchor, no baselining item exists and extract is pickable a minute
903	  after its own yes. Nothing is spent, no task claims a run, and the engine
904	  still never knows what baselining is — `after` names a task id, and the
905	  pick filter reads item states, generically. §12's exclusive-claim
906	  machinery (and its stated throughput cost) deletes. `Blocked-by` remains
907	  the right edge for what it is: dependencies on items that *terminate*
908	  (follow-ups, fan-ins).
909	- **Fan-out with a fan-in.** Fanning out is creating N items (§8). The fan-in
910	  is one more item — the status/aggregation task — created `Blocked-by` all N.
911	  It readies only when every child converged, and its precondition/work step read
912	  the children's outcome labels to report or escalate. "Getting the status of
913	  a fan-out" stops being a bespoke sweep and becomes an ordinary task whose
914	  edges the scheduler run already evaluates.
915	
916	**Readiness has a second site: whoever closes an item re-checks its dependents
917	in code** (F1, reopened by the owner 2026-08-15 — reversing the 2026-08-13
918	decline, and amending §15.8's "dependency readiness is the scheduler run's alone" in
919	siting, not in principle). On closing an item, the executor or agent doing the
920	closing evaluates every open `task:status:blocked` item naming it: `Blocked-by` all
921	closed and `Not-before` passed flips the dependent to `task:status:waiting-for-executor`, and a
922	drain follows — so a chain link or a fan-in proceeds within minutes of its
923	upstream converging instead of waiting out the scheduler run. What changed since the
924	decline: under the work-as-work model the ~1h/link quantization stacks on
925	drain occupancy, so a three-link chain on a busy morning trailed into the
926	afternoon. The scheduler run's readiness job stays exactly as it was, as the backstop —
927	a close by hand runs no engine code, and a missed re-check costs a scheduler run of
928	latency, never correctness (SCENARIOS S33, and S4's tightened chain timing).
929	
930	Native GitHub issue dependencies (blocked-by/blocking — GA since Aug 2025,
931	API- and webhook-supported) and sub-issues *mirror* these fields: the scheduler run
932	writes the native edge alongside the body field, buying the dependency UI for
933	free ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2). The body fields remain the truth the scheduler run
934	parses — they are portable to any tracker with issues, labels, and comments,
935	which is the platform-agnosticism the sketch asks for. One vendored module owns
936	parse/serialize of the two fields; nothing else touches them.
937	
938	Cycles: the scheduler run readies nothing in a `Blocked-by` cycle, forever, and the
939	stale escalation (§11) surfaces it as `needs-human` + `task:status:needs-human-action` after ~2 periods — the
940	same convergence-not-prevention posture as the rest of the system. The scheduler run
941	does not attempt cycle detection; the janitor's health review may.
942	
943	## 10. Capacity and platform-agnosticism
944	
945	The default deployment stays one vendored cron workflow — the repo's only
946	cron, rule unchanged — containing the scheduler-run job and a drain (the scheduler run goes
947	first; the drain then starts an executor for what it created, which keeps the
948	common case's latency at zero even without events). **The drain dispatches
949	rather than executes**, which is how it leaves the scheduler run's concurrency group
950	below: this job's success means the drain was started, never that it
951	finished. Event triggers (`task:status:waiting-for-executor` labeled)
952	give urgent and hand-created items sub-minute pickup — with one platform fact
953	worth knowing: a label written by a workflow's own `GITHUB_TOKEN` emits no
954	triggering event (GitHub's recursion guard), so events only ever come from
955	*foreign* tokens — a human, a CLI on a PAT, an agent session. The drain being
956	in-run is what makes that harmless; it is the structural delivery, events the
957	sugar.
958	
959	**The capacity model, honestly** (work-as-work review, 2026-08-15): the work
960	step is the work, so throughput is run *occupancy* — one run, one item, and
961	the queue drains as a chain of runs. The CCR sessions runs hand off
962	parallelize for free; the executor-side work does not. So executor width is
963	the primary capacity parameter, not a garnish: scale with a matrix width for
964	parallel executor jobs, or with executors outside Actions entirely — the
965	contract is "issue read/write plus the repo checkout at HEAD", so a runner
966	anywhere with a token qualifies. The chain itself is **self-re-dispatch**:
967	`workflow_dispatch` is one of the two event types a `GITHUB_TOKEN` *can*
968	fire, so a run that ends with ready items left re-dispatches the executor
969	workflow and a fresh run continues.
970	One fairness note, accepted at today's scale: the randomized pick (§6.1)
971	removes any *systematic* head domination, but a heavy item still occupies its
972	run for the full work bound while light tasks wait out the chain — a sentence
973	here rather than machinery, until it is measured.
974	
975	**What starts an executor run is an enumerable list, and each cause is on the
976	record** (2026-08-15, and the sim asserts it — S34): (1) **the scheduler run's own
977	drain job** — the guaranteed delivery, started by the cron workflow's job
978	graph (`needs: scheduler run`), no event involved; (2) **a `task:status:waiting-for-executor`/`task:urgent`
979	label event** — foreign tokens only, the latency sugar; (3) **the close-time
980	drain** — whoever converges an item triggers a drain when anything is
981	pickable after its readiness re-check (§9); (4) **self-re-dispatch** — a run
982	that ends its one item with others still pickable dispatches a fresh run;
983	(5) **the failure continuation** — a run that dies (crash, timeout,
984	cancellation, runner loss) never reaches its re-dispatch, so the executor
985	workflow carries a second job, `needs: execute` with `if: failure() ||
986	cancelled()`, which the platform runs on a fresh runner and whose one step
987	re-dispatches — a dead run stalls the train by ~a minute, not until the next
988	cron fire (S36). The continuation carries **a depth, capped at three**
989	(engine-side, 2026-08-20, not from the review): a run that dies at *startup*
990	— a broken engine, a revoked token — dies identically every time, so an
991	unguarded continuation dispatches itself for as long as that lasts. At the
992	cap the chain stops and escalates to the repo's workflow-failure issue rather
993	than going quiet, because a queue that has stopped draining is the one
994	failure where every individual run looks like an ordinary death. Causes 3–5 ride `workflow_dispatch`, which the default
995	`GITHUB_TOKEN` *is* permitted to fire — the explicit exemption in the same
996	recursion guard that suppresses its label events — so no wider credential is
997	involved.
998	
999	**The scheduler run must never wait on a drain** (work-as-work review, 2026-08-15).
1000	The heartbeat retires the sub-hour cap on executor runs (§6), and a long
1001	drain sharing the scheduler run's serializing `concurrency` group would then hold the
1002	next cron fire — instantiation, readiness and the leash reclaim all stalling
1003	behind the very work they schedule. So the serialization the double-scheduler run
1004	guard needs (S6) scopes to the **scheduler run alone**, and executor work runs outside
1005	it: the drain leaves the cron workflow's concurrency group (its own group, or
1006	the separate executor workflow via dispatch). A deployment where the drain
1007	can still block the scheduler run is mis-wired even while nothing visibly fails. The
1008	engine took the dispatch option, which has a second effect worth naming: the
1009	drain job runs no task code, so it holds **no secrets at all** — the executor
1010	workflow is the only place they live, with nothing left beside it to leak
1011	into.
1012	
1013	Executor identity is self-declared in claim comments; the system never
1014	enumerates executors, which is why adding one requires telling no one.
1015	
1016	## 11. Recovery — what the janitor keeps, what dies
1017	
1018	| failure | today | proposed |
1019	|---|---|---|
1020	| scheduler/scheduler run miss or late fire | run-ledger catch-up math | same property from the occurrence guard (§5) — the next scheduler run instantiates the most recent occurrence only |
1021	| double scheduler run | concurrency group + slot-title search | concurrency group + occurrence-guard search (same window, same answer) |
1022	| lost label event | janitor re-arm (remove/re-add), 20-min grace, bounded by stale escalation | **retired** — executors poll on the scheduler run's cron; events are latency sugar, never the only delivery |
1023	| duplicate events / racing executors | claim lease on one implicit executor | same lease, N executors — the loser picks a different item |
1024	| executor died mid-claim | — (executor was a session; janitor reclaimed via `agent-running`) | **the scheduler run** (owner, 2026-08-13): `task:status:running-executor` with no activity past ~1h → strip to `task:status:waiting-for-executor` with a comment, so a dead executor's item is back in the queue within ~2h rather than ~25h. An executor iteration is minutes, not hours, and a lease checked once a day is not a short lease |

baselining runs first, extract and promote follow *the same night* in
  order; on the routine night where baselining's precondition declines at
  its anchor, no baselining item exists and extract is pickable a minute
  after its own yes. Nothing is spent, no task claims a run, and the engine
  still never knows what baselining is — `after` names a task id, and the
  pick filter reads item states, generically. §12's exclusive-claim
  machinery (and its stated throughput cost) deletes. `Blocked-by` remains
  the right edge for what it is: dependencies on items that *terminate*
  (follow-ups, fan-ins).
- **Fan-out with a fan-in.** Fanning out is creating N items (§8). The fan-in
  is one more item — the status/aggregation task — created `Blocked-by` all N.
  It readies only when every child converged, and its precondition/work step read
  the children's outcome labels to report or escalate. "Getting the status of
  a fan-out" stops being a bespoke sweep and becomes an ordinary task whose
  edges the scheduler run already evaluates.

**Readiness has a second site: whoever closes an item re-checks its dependents
in code** (F1, reopened by the owner 2026-08-15 — reversing the 2026-08-13
decline, and amending §15.8's "dependency readiness is the scheduler run's alone" in
siting, not in principle). On closing an item, the executor or agent doing the
closing evaluates every open `task:status:blocked` item naming it: `Blocked-by` all
closed and `Not-before` passed flips the dependent to `task:status:waiting-for-executor`, and a
drain follows — so a chain link or a fan-in proceeds within minutes of its
upstream converging instead of waiting out the scheduler run. What changed since the
decline: under the work-as-work model the ~1h/link quantization stacks on
drain occupancy, so a three-link chain on a busy morning trailed into the
afternoon. The scheduler run's readiness job stays exactly as it was, as the backstop —
a close by hand runs no engine code, and a missed re-check costs a scheduler run of
latency, never correctness (SCENARIOS S33, and S4's tightened chain timing).

Native GitHub issue dependencies (blocked-by/blocking — GA since Aug 2025,
API- and webhook-supported) and sub-issues *mirror* these fields: the scheduler run
writes the native edge alongside the body field, buying the dependency UI for
free ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2). The body fields remain the truth the scheduler run
parses — they are portable to any tracker with issues, labels, and comments,
which is the platform-agnosticism the sketch asks for. One vendored module owns
parse/serialize of the two fields; nothing else touches them.

Cycles: the scheduler run readies nothing in a `Blocked-by` cycle, forever, and the
stale escalation (§11) surfaces it as `needs-human` + `task:status:needs-human-action` after ~2 periods — the
same convergence-not-prevention posture as the rest of the system. The scheduler run
does not attempt cycle detection; the janitor's health review may.

## 10. Capacity and platform-agnosticism

The default deployment stays one vendored cron workflow — the repo's only
cron, rule unchanged — containing the scheduler-run job and a drain (the scheduler run goes
first; the drain then starts an executor for what it created, which keeps the
common case's latency at zero even without events). **The drain dispatches
rather than executes**, which is how it leaves the scheduler run's concurrency group
below: this job's success means the drain was started, never that it
finished. Event triggers (`task:status:waiting-for-executor` labeled)
give urgent and hand-created items sub-minute pickup — with one platform fact
worth knowing: a label written by a workflow's own `GITHUB_TOKEN` emits no
triggering event (GitHub's recursion guard), so events only ever come from
*foreign* tokens — a human, a CLI on a PAT, an agent session. The drain being
in-run is what makes that harmless; it is the structural delivery, events the
sugar.

**The capacity model, honestly** (work-as-work review, 2026-08-15): the work
step is the work, so throughput is run *occupancy* — one run, one item, and
the queue drains as a chain of runs. The CCR sessions runs hand off
parallelize for free; the executor-side work does not. So executor width is
the primary capacity parameter, not a garnish: scale with a matrix width for
parallel executor jobs, or with executors outside Actions entirely — the
contract is "issue read/write plus the repo checkout at HEAD", so a runner
anywhere with a token qualifies. The chain itself is **self-re-dispatch**:
`workflow_dispatch` is one of the two event types a `GITHUB_TOKEN` *can*
fire, so a run that ends with ready items left re-dispatches the executor
workflow and a fresh run continues.
One fairness note, accepted at today's scale: the randomized pick (§6.1)
removes any *systematic* head domination, but a heavy item still occupies its
run for the full work bound while light tasks wait out the chain — a sentence
here rather than machinery, until it is measured.

**What starts an executor run is an enumerable list, and each cause is on the
record** (2026-08-15, and the sim asserts it — S34): (1) **the scheduler run's own
drain job** — the guaranteed delivery, started by the cron workflow's job
graph (`needs: scheduler run`), no event involved; (2) **a `task:status:waiting-for-executor`/`task:urgent`
label event** — foreign tokens only, the latency sugar; (3) **the close-time
drain** — whoever converges an item triggers a drain when anything is
pickable after its readiness re-check (§9); (4) **self-re-dispatch** — a run
that ends its one item with others still pickable dispatches a fresh run;
(5) **the failure continuation** — a run that dies (crash, timeout,
cancellation, runner loss) never reaches its re-dispatch, so the executor
workflow carries a second job, `needs: execute` with `if: failure() ||
cancelled()`, which the platform runs on a fresh runner and whose one step
re-dispatches — a dead run stalls the train by ~a minute, not until the next
cron fire (S36). The continuation carries **a depth, capped at three**
(engine-side, 2026-08-20, not from the review): a run that dies at *startup*
— a broken engine, a revoked token — dies identically every time, so an
unguarded continuation dispatches itself for as long as that lasts. At the
cap the chain stops and escalates to the repo's workflow-failure issue rather
than going quiet, because a queue that has stopped draining is the one
failure where every individual run looks like an ordinary death. Causes 3–5 ride `workflow_dispatch`, which the default
`GITHUB_TOKEN` *is* permitted to fire — the explicit exemption in the same
recursion guard that suppresses its label events — so no wider credential is
involved.

**The scheduler run must never wait on a drain** (work-as-work review, 2026-08-15).
The heartbeat retires the sub-hour cap on executor runs (§6), and a long
drain sharing the scheduler run's serializing `concurrency` group would then hold the
next cron fire — instantiation, readiness and the leash reclaim all stalling
behind the very work they schedule. So the serialization the double-scheduler run
guard needs (S6) scopes to the **scheduler run alone**, and executor work runs outside
it: the drain leaves the cron workflow's concurrency group (its own group, or
the separate executor workflow via dispatch). A deployment where the drain
can still block the scheduler run is mis-wired even while nothing visibly fails. The
engine took the dispatch option, which has a second effect worth naming: the
drain job runs no task code, so it holds **no secrets at all** — the executor
workflow is the only place they live, with nothing left beside it to leak
into.

Executor identity is self-declared in claim comments; the system never
enumerates executors, which is why adding one requires telling no one.

# endpoint's token secret, into the step env below by name — the scheduler run and the
# janitor get none, because they never execute task code. Code-work is the only task
# code that ever sees a value; the agent hop carries nothing.
#

# independently leased, so a second job, a matrix width, or a runner outside
# Actions entirely all work — the executor's whole interface is issue read/write
# plus the repo at HEAD.

  issues:
    types: [labeled]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      continuation_depth:

        required: false
        type: string

  contents: write
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  actions: write

    # (#1119). A workflow's event trigger names label strings LITERALLY — nothing
    # here decodes — so this list is the one place the migration's two vocabularies
    # must both appear, and dropping the legacy spelling early makes every item an
    # older engine readies wait for the hourly scheduler run instead of starting now.

      github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:status:waiting-for-executor'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:ready'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:urgent'

    # than length. What is left here is a backstop against a wedged runner, well

          CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}

  # its own re-dispatch, so without this the queue would sit until the next cron

  # (DESIGN §10, S36), and its one step fires that dispatch instead: the

  # chain stops and SAYS SO on the repo's workflow-failure issue: a queue that has
  # quietly stopped draining is the one failure nothing else here would surface,
  # since every individual run looks like an ordinary death.

    permissions:
      actions: write
      issues: write

            const ref = context.payload.repository?.default_branch

            // and dispatching a fourth would spend the day proving it. Escalate to
            // the same one-open-issue surface the scheduler's own failures use, and
            // let the hourly scheduler run be what tries again.

# Claudinite work-item queue — the generator's scheduler run and its drain (tasks-dispatch
# DESIGN §5, §10). This is the repo's ONLY cron, and it replaces the slot
# scheduler's content at the same path when `taskScheduler.dispatch` is `"queue"`
# — same file, same hashed minute, different mechanism, so the one-cron rule and
# every reader that knows this workflow by name keep holding.
#
# A thin shim: all logic lives in the vendored engine, so this file changes
# rarely. The minute below is a placeholder; bootstrap and the wiring converge
# rewrite it to this repo's stable hashed minute in :10–:50, computed by
# `node engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs <owner/repo>`.
#
# TWO JOBS, IN ORDER. The scheduler run is pure label mechanics over the issue list —
# instantiate each task's standing item at its anchor, ready what is due, reclaim
# dead executor claims — and evaluates no precondition and collects no signal. The
# drain then STARTS an executor run for what the scheduler run just created, which is what
# keeps the common case's latency at zero even with no `labeled` event delivered.
# Lost events are therefore never the only delivery — they are latency sugar,
# which is what retires the re-arm.
#
# The drain dispatches rather than executes, and that is the point: this workflow's
# concurrency group serializes SCHEDULER RUNS, and an executor run inside it would make each
# hour's scheduler run queue behind the previous hour's work — which the heartbeat, by making
# long work legal, turned from theoretical into likely (DESIGN §15.16).
#
# `workflow_dispatch` is not a convenience: it is the never-wait-for-the-cron
# lever every forced run, migration and validation burst depends on. Its one
# input is how that lever reaches ACROSS repos: the fleet enforcer dispatches
# this workflow naming the tasks to run now, and this member wakes its own
# standing items with its own token (DESIGN §8). The alternative — the enforcer
# editing every member's issues directly — would widen the fleet PAT to issue
# writes on every repository, for a job the member can do for itself.
name: Claudinite scheduler

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '44 * * * *'
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      wake:
        description: 'Task ids to run now (`pack/task` or a bare task name, space-separated) — wakes each one’s standing item regardless of its anchor'
        required: false
        type: string

# One scheduler run at a time, always. The scheduler run's duplicate-standing-item self-heal is
# written assuming exactly this — it closes every open family item but the oldest,
# which is safe precisely because two scheduler runs never run at once.
concurrency:
  group: claudinite-scheduler-run
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: write        # read the repo + vendored engine; a task's code_work pushes its delivery branch
  issues: write          # create / label / comment / close work items — the queue itself
  pull-requests: write   # a task's code_work opens its PR and arms auto-merge
  actions: write         # dispatch a workflow a task drives (creating a workflow_dispatch event needs write; `read` silently 403s the POST)

jobs:
  scheduler-run:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Instantiate, ready and reclaim work items
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          CLAUDINITE_WAKE: ${{ inputs.wake }}
          # The operator hold (DESIGN §8): set this repo variable to `true` and
          # every entry point exits at its first act, having fired nothing.
          CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL: ${{ vars.CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL }}
        run: node engine/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run.mjs

  # THE POST-SCHEDULER RUN DRAIN, DISPATCHED RATHER THAN RUN HERE (DESIGN §10, §15.16).
  # The scheduler run's concurrency group serializes scheduler runs — its duplicate-item self-heal
  # depends on that — and a drain running inside the group would make every hour's
  # scheduler run queue behind the previous hour's work. Since the heartbeat made long work
  # legal, that is no longer a theoretical wait. So the drain is a `workflow_dispatch`
  # of the executor workflow: it starts in its own group, on its own runner, and
  # this job's success means "the drain was started", never "the drain finished".
  #
  # This is still the guaranteed delivery. A label event may be lost; this fires
  # every hour whatever happens.
  drain:
    needs: scheduler-run
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      actions: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            await github.rest.actions.createWorkflowDispatch({
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              workflow_id: 'claudinite-executor.yml',
              ref: context.payload.repository?.default_branch
                ?? context.ref.replace('refs/heads/', ''),
            });
            core.info('dispatched the executor to drain whatever this scheduler run created');

  # A scheduled run reaches no one when it goes red, so escalate a whole-run
  # failure to a human-visible `workflow-failure` issue. Converges to ONE open
  # issue by a fixed title (create-or-comment), and ensures the label first since a
  # first-run failure may precede any label-ensure.
  report-failure:
    needs: [scheduler-run, drain]
    if: failure()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const { owner, repo } = context.repo;
            const title = 'Claudinite scheduler run failed';
            // The platform reporting its own failure IS an origin (`task:origin:github`),
            // parked in the `failure` lane — the one a person diagnoses (#1119).
            const labels = ['workflow-failure', 'task:origin:github', 'task:status:needs-human-failure'];
            const ensure = [
              { name: 'workflow-failure', color: 'b60205', description: 'Claudinite scheduler: a scheduler run or task failed' },
              { name: 'task:origin:github', color: 'd4c5f9', description: 'Claudinite queue: filed by the platform itself — a workflow reporting its own failure' },
              { name: 'task:status:needs-human-failure', color: 'b60205', description: 'Claudinite queue: parked — the run broke, diagnose and fix' },
            ];
            for (const l of ensure) await github.rest.issues.createLabel({ owner, repo, ...l }).catch(() => {});
            const run = `${context.serverUrl}/${owner}/${repo}/actions/runs/${context.runId}`;
            const body = `The Claudinite scheduler run/drain run failed: ${run}`;
            const found = await github.rest.search.issuesAndPullRequests({ q: `repo:${owner}/${repo} is:issue is:open in:title "${title}"` });
            if (found.data.total_count > 0) await github.rest.issues.createComment({ owner, repo, issue_number: found.data.items[0].number, body });
            else await github.rest.issues.create({ owner, repo, title, labels, body });

input.title: Sim: batched executor drain, conditional drain dispatch, Action-executions accounting + day scenarios
input.body:
The simulator half of #1212, per the sim's own working discipline (change the simulator first, let red tests name what the design change breaks, then update the prose and tests together):

- `sim.mjs`: one executor run drains until empty (the settle continues the same run instead of re-dispatching); the scheduler run schedules its drain only when something is pickable; the hold is re-checked between items; `actionExecutions()` counts workflow runs (scheduler + executor, by trigger — a suspended start still bills).
- Scenarios: a day's worth of scheduled + ad-hoc work asserting the total invocation count, and a quiet day asserting the cron floor alone. S34/S36 rewritten to the batched-drain invariants.
- DESIGN.md §10/§15 amended (the §15.22 reversal recorded), SCENARIOS.md and the sim README/coverage map updated.

content.text: {"id":"5221277631","url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1213"}

input.title: Engine: executor drains until empty; scheduler drain job dispatches only when work is pickable
input.body:
The engine half of #1212, behind the simulator/DESIGN change (#1213) — the deployed code and the vendored workflow stubs still implement one-item-per-run and the unconditional drain until this lands:

- `engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs`: after an item settles, pick the next in the same run instead of self-re-dispatching; re-read `CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL` via the API between items (env delivery is start-only), so the hold parks the run at most one item later. The failure-continuation job keeps its role for a run that dies with items still queued.
- `engine/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run.mjs` + `.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml` (canon copy and stub in the same commit): the drain job dispatches the executor only when the scheduler run reports something pickable (a job output), instead of every hour.
- `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml`: header contract updated from "one run performs one item"; timeout re-sized for a batched drain.

Both workflow stubs are fleet-vendored surfaces — sweep for cross-repo callers of the dispatch protocol before reshaping anything they declare (#929, #801).

content.text: Now the §10 body prose — the capacity model and the enumerable causes list:

input.old_string:
The default deployment stays one vendored cron workflow — the repo's only
cron, rule unchanged — containing the scheduler-run job and a drain (the scheduler run goes
first; the drain then starts an executor for what it created, which keeps the
common case's latency at zero even without events). **The drain dispatches
rather than executes**, which is how it leaves the scheduler run's concurrency group
below: this job's success means the drain was started, never that it
finished. Event triggers (`task:status:waiting-for-executor` labeled)
input.new_string:

common case's latency at zero even without events). **The drain dispatches
rather than executes**, which is how it leaves the scheduler run's concurrency group
below: this job's success means the drain was started, never that it
finished. **And it dispatches only when the scheduler run's parting look at
the queue found something pickable** (§15.30): every workflow run is a billed
invocation whatever it finds, so an idle hour costs the cron's one run — the
guaranteed delivery is unweakened, because anything an event failed to
deliver is exactly what that parting look sees.

input.old_string:
**The capacity model, honestly** (work-as-work review, 2026-08-15): the work
step is the work, so throughput is run *occupancy* — one run, one item, and
the queue drains as a chain of runs. The CCR sessions runs hand off
parallelize for free; the executor-side work does not. So executor width is
the primary capacity parameter, not a garnish: scale with a matrix width for
parallel executor jobs, or with executors outside Actions entirely — the
contract is "issue read/write plus the repo checkout at HEAD", so a runner
anywhere with a token qualifies. The chain itself is **self-re-dispatch**:
`workflow_dispatch` is one of the two event types a `GITHUB_TOKEN` *can*
fire, so a run that ends with ready items left re-dispatches the executor
workflow and a fresh run continues.

input.old_string:
**What starts an executor run is an enumerable list, and each cause is on the
record** (2026-08-15, and the sim asserts it — S34): (1) **the scheduler run's own
drain job** — the guaranteed delivery, started by the cron workflow's job
graph (`needs: scheduler run`), no event involved; (2) **a `task:status:waiting-for-executor`/`task:urgent`
label event** — foreign tokens only, the latency sugar; (3) **the close-time
drain** — whoever converges an item triggers a drain when anything is
pickable after its readiness re-check (§9); (4) **self-re-dispatch** — a run
that ends its one item with others still pickable dispatches a fresh run;
(5) **the failure continuation** — a run that dies (crash, timeout,
cancellation, runner loss) never reaches its re-dispatch, so the executor
workflow carries a second job, `needs: execute` with `if: failure() ||
cancelled()`, which the platform runs on a fresh runner and whose one step
re-dispatches — a dead run stalls the train by ~a minute, not until the next
cron fire (S36). The continuation carries **a depth, capped at three**
(engine-side, 2026-08-20, not from the review): a run that dies at *startup*
— a broken engine, a revoked token — dies identically every time, so an
unguarded continuation dispatches itself for as long as that lasts. At the
cap the chain stops and escalates to the repo's workflow-failure issue rather
than going quiet, because a queue that has stopped draining is the one
failure where every individual run looks like an ordinary death. Causes 3–5 ride `workflow_dispatch`, which the default
`GITHUB_TOKEN` *is* permitted to fire — the explicit exemption in the same
recursion guard that suppresses its label events — so no wider credential is
involved.

single cancellation can *never* mean is "stop the system" — the scheduler run and
  events keep spawning runs — so that intent gets its own lever:
- **Suspending the whole queue is `CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL`** (owner,
  2026-08-16): a repo Actions **variable** (`vars.*`, stamped into each
  workflow's env by the wiring — settable in the UI or over the API, **no
  commit**), which every Claudinite workflow — scheduler run and executor alike —
  checks as its *first act* and, when true, exits cleanly having fired
  nothing. The train parks at most one hop after suspension (an already
  in-flight continuation may fire one re-dispatch; that fresh run sees the
  variable and parks). Suspension gates workflow *starts* only: in-flight
  runs and agent sessions finish on their own — cancel those by hand if the
  hold is urgent — and items freeze exactly where they are, no labels
  touched, which is what makes the hold stateless. This is not dormancy:
  `dormant` is a *declared standing state* in tracked config, a commit,
  read by the same gates; the suspend variable is the instant, out-of-band
  operational hold. (S37.)
- **Resuming is clearing the variable — recovery needs no lever of its own.**
  The next cron scheduler run performs the entire self-heal unaided: its reclaim job
  frees the claims of runs killed during the hold (their heartbeats long
  silent), its readiness job wakes whatever came due, and its drain picks the
  queue back up. An operator who won't wait the ≤1h dispatches the
  **scheduler** workflow by hand — the scheduler run-plus-drain pair, *not* the bare
  executor, whose run would drain ready items but skip the reclaim/ready
  half that makes resume complete. (S38.)
- **`manual` tasks** are simply tasks the scheduler run never instantiates: their items
  are only ever created by hand or by other tasks. The frequency token
  survives; the special-case slot resolution for it dies.
- **Fan-out across repos** is the enforcer creating one item per member repo

2026-08-15's one-item run: Actions bills per job with minutes rounded up, so
the run count is the cost): claim an item, see it through to its settle
(close, hand-off, or failure), then pick the next in the same run, ending
only when nothing is pickable. Items still settle **one at a time** — the
serial occupancy of §10 is unchanged — and a platform kill still loses at
most the *current* item's progress: the already-settled items stand, and the
failure continuation (§10) drains the remainder on a fresh runner. Each
item's claim is independently leased, so executor concurrency
is safe at any width.

705	bound tying the run to its leash — `timeout-minutes` ≤ the executing leash, so
706	the platform killed a hung runner before its claim was reaped — **retires with
707	the heartbeat** (2026-08-15): it capped every run at under an hour, which the
708	work-as-work model cannot accept. The stalled-worker lesson
709	([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2) is now held by three smaller pieces instead: a
710	*dead* runner stops heartbeating and is reclaimed within ~the leash; a *wedged
711	work subprocess* is killed by the work's own declared timeout (the contract's
712	existing bound), after which the executor converges the failure; and a
713	*reclaimed-but-alive* runner abandons at its next transition, because the
714	executor re-verifies its own lease at every state change (§11). The run's
715	`timeout-minutes` is then sized to the work it may legally do — the largest
716	single work bound it can pick — not to the leash.
717	
718	**Idempotency, honestly (owner concern, 2026-08-13: "I'm not sure we can
719	guarantee all tasks to be idempotent").** Agreed — and the design does not
720	require it. The queue literature's blanket "make handlers idempotent" applies
721	to systems where duplicate *invocations* reach the handler; here the executor
722	claim collapses duplicate pickups **before work starts** (§6.2) and at-most-once
723	invocation means no duplicate ever reaches the agent hop (§6.6), so what tasks
724	must actually tolerate is much narrower:
725	
726	- **The work step must be re-entrant** — a *sequential* re-run after a
727	  crash-and-reclaim (§6.5). That is convergence ("check what exists, continue
728	  from there"), not idempotency, and it is already required of the work today.

the heartbeat** (2026-08-15): it capped every run at under an hour, which the
work-as-work model cannot accept. The stalled-worker lesson
([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2) is now held by three smaller pieces instead: a
*dead* runner stops heartbeating and is reclaimed within ~the leash; a *wedged
work subprocess* is killed by the work's own declared timeout (the contract's
existing bound), after which the executor converges the failure; and a
*reclaimed-but-alive* runner abandons at its next transition, because the
executor re-verifies its own lease at every state change (§11). The run's
`timeout-minutes` is then sized to the work it may legally do — the largest
single work bound it can pick — not to the leash.

**Idempotency, honestly (owner concern, 2026-08-13: "I'm not sure we can
guarantee all tasks to be idempotent").** Agreed — and the design does not
require it. The queue literature's blanket "make handlers idempotent" applies
to systems where duplicate *invocations* reach the handler; here the executor
claim collapses duplicate pickups **before work starts** (§6.2) and at-most-once
invocation means no duplicate ever reaches the agent hop (§6.6), so what tasks
must actually tolerate is much narrower:

- **The work step must be re-entrant** — a *sequential* re-run after a
  crash-and-reclaim (§6.5). That is convergence ("check what exists, continue
  from there"), not idempotency, and it is already required of the work today.

for a fresh repo, baselining's wiring converge for an established one — and
its wiring is exactly four things, all idempotent, all from the vendored
engine at HEAD:

1. **Labels**, create-if-missing: `task:status:waiting-for-executor/blocked/executing/agent/urgent`,
   `needs-human` and its four sub-labels (until #1050 retires the bare label),
   and the terminal pair `task:status:done`/`task:status:rejected`. Nothing ensures
   `outcome:delivered` — nothing applies it; decoders still read it and every
   other legacy spelling.
2. **Two vendored workflows**: the scheduler run (cron at the repo's stable hashed
   minute, plus `workflow_dispatch` so an operator or a migration never waits
   for the cron), and the executor (invoked as the scheduler run's drain job and by
   `labeled` events on `task:status:waiting-for-executor`/`task:urgent`; carries the stamped
   secrets env — below).
3. **Config**: `taskScheduler.dispatch: "queue"`, the endpoint map (§12), the
   anchor schedule.
4. **Nothing else** — no seed items, no ledger to initialize. The first scheduler run
   after wiring creates every task's first item `task:status:blocked` until its next

763	run chaining a fresh one via `workflow_dispatch`, which the default
764	`GITHUB_TOKEN` may fire; `failure-redispatch` — the workflow's continuation

766	ready** (owner, same day — the stale-ready escalation is period-scale, so
767	nothing leaned on oldest-first), seeded in the sim so scenarios replay

774	  dry with no second cron fire involved.

776	  dies, or times out — what will cause the third executor to start?"*): five
777	  tasks with work; the run executing one of them dies two minutes in. Its
778	  ordinary re-dispatch never fires — it fires at run *end* — and the answer

### S34/S36 — run granularity, and what causes the next run (F23)

The first simulator brought up to this review still modeled the executor as an
instantaneous loop: all picked items' work phases started in the same virtual
instant, nothing bounded a run, and no test could say *which run* did *what* —
exactly the shape F21 warned about, reproduced in the model meant to catch it
(owner question, 2026-08-15: *"asserted that each executor run completes just
one task from the queue? Have you simulated what causes the next executor
run?"*). The sim now models runs as first-class objects. **A run performs one
item** — not a bound but the executor's essence (owner, same day: *"An
executor performs a task. It's not a current value. It's the essence of
it."*): claim, see it to its settle (roll, close, hand-off, failure), end.
**Every run records its cause**: `scheduler-run-drain` — the cron workflow's own drain
job, started by the job graph, no event involved; `label-event` — a foreign
token's `task:status:waiting-for-executor`/`task:urgent`; `close-drain` — the converge path, when
its readiness re-check leaves something pickable; `re-dispatch` — a finished
run chaining a fresh one via `workflow_dispatch`, which the default
`GITHUB_TOKEN` may fire; `failure-redispatch` — the workflow's continuation
job (S36 below). And the pick order is **urgent first, then random among the
ready** (owner, same day — the stale-ready escalation is period-scale, so
nothing leaned on oldest-first), seeded in the sim so scenarios replay
identically.

- **S34** (two tasks with real work plus the day's rolls): every completed
  run settled **at most one item**, the working runs exactly one; both work
  items converged well inside the hour, so the record must show — and does —
  `scheduler-run-drain` first, then `re-dispatch`/`close-drain` chaining the queue
  dry with no second cron fire involved.
- **S36** (the broken train — owner question: *"the 2nd executor fails, or
  dies, or times out — what will cause the third executor to start?"*): five
  tasks with work; the run executing one of them dies two minutes in. Its
  ordinary re-dispatch never fires — it fires at run *end* — and the answer
  is the **failure-continuation job**: `needs: execute`, `if: failure() ||
  cancelled()`, run by the platform on a fresh runner even after a timeout,
  cancellation, or runner loss, its one step re-dispatching the workflow. The
  test asserts the four unaffected items drained within minutes with no cron
  fire involved, the crashed item alone waited out the leash reclaim and then
  converged, and no run ever settled more than its one item. The hourly scheduler run
  drain remains the backstop for the case where the whole run vanishes,
  continuation job included.

### S37/S38 — the operator hold, and resume (owner, 2026-08-16)

The cancellation-intent question: a user cancelling one executor run almost
always means *"this run is stalled — let the system move on"*, and the
mechanism already treats it exactly so (cancellation = crash: the failure
continuation keeps the train moving, the leash frees the item). The intent it
can never express is *"stop processing"*, so that one is a lever:
**`CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL`**, a repo Actions variable every Claudinite
workflow checks as its first act, exiting cleanly having fired nothing.

- **S37 (the hold)**: five tasks mid-drain; the variable set at 04:30. No
  pick, no evaluation happens after the hold — but an in-flight run finishes
  its item (suspension gates *starts*, not running work), the in-flight
  continuation's one re-dispatch parks at its first act, every later cron
  fire exits as a recorded `suspended-skip`, and every never-picked item
  freezes as `task:status:waiting-for-executor`, untouched — the hold is stateless.
- **S38 (cancel + suspend, then resume)**: the user cancels a stalled run
  mid-work AND suspends before its continuation lands — intent 2 overrides
  intent 1's train, the continuation's re-dispatch parks. Hours later the
  variable is cleared, **and nothing else is done**: the next cron scheduler run alone
  reclaims the cancelled run's long-silent claim, readies what came due, and
  its drain converges the whole queue. The impatient path — a hand-dispatched
  *scheduler* run (scheduler run + drain), not a bare executor run — is the same
  recovery a minute sooner; a bare executor would drain ready items but skip
  the reclaim/ready half.

## J. The triage split (owner, 2026-08-19)

`needs-human` was one word for fifteen different situations, and a person

  skipped its drain.

  tasks with work; the one drain run dies two minutes into its fourth item.

  test asserts the unaffected items drained within minutes with no cron
  fire involved, the crashed item alone waited out the leash reclaim and then

  continuation job included.

## N. Invocation cost — the batched drain and the executions accounting (owner, 2026-08-22, #1212)

Actions bills each job's runtime rounded **up** to the next minute, so a
day's cost is the workflow-run count, not the minutes worked — and the
one-item run (§15.22) paid a whole invocation of checkout, setup and rounding
per item, with the hourly drain dispatched even into an empty queue. The
reversal (§15.30): a run drains until nothing is pickable, the drain job
dispatches only when the scheduler run left something pickable, and the hold
is re-read between items. The accounting (`actionExecutions()`) counts every
billed run — a suspended start included, since the runner still spins up to
read the hold — by workflow and, for the executor, by recorded trigger. S34,
S36 and S37 above replay under the new run boundary; the two scenarios here
pin the bill itself.

### S65 — a working day's bill

A full day of scheduled work — the 02:00/03:00/04:00 morning chain, tidy,
a release — plus ad-hoc work: a marked request and a hand-created item of a
manual task. Seven pieces of work converge for exactly **29 invocations**:
the cron's 24 scheduler runs (the floor), one drain per hour that had work
(four — the 04:00 anchor's three items settle in the one 04:17 run), and the
hand-created item's one label event. The 20 hours with nothing pickable
dispatched no executor at all.

### S66 — the quiet day's floor

No signals, no items: **24 invocations**, the hourly cron alone — every
scheduler run skipped its drain, and no executor runner ever started. Under
the retired shape the same day cost 48.

content.content:
886	### The prose-only findings (no scenario can carry them)
887	
888	- **F19 — a long drain starves the scheduler run.** The drain job shares the cron
889	  workflow's serializing `concurrency` group, so once the heartbeat legalizes
890	  multi-hour work, a busy drain holds the next hourly fire — instantiation,
891	  readiness and the leash reclaim all stall behind the very work they
892	  schedule. Fixed in DESIGN §10: the serialization scopes to the scheduler run alone;
893	  executor work runs outside it. The sim cannot see workflow concurrency
894	  (unsimulated-world row); the migration burst verifies the wiring.

  agentless run — the majority, under this review's premise — the item's
  terminal comment is the only durable trace, so it must carry the
  `claudinite-task-exec` record and every artifact the work created. DESIGN
  §6.5 makes it contract.

input.title: Batched executor drain: invocations are the cost unit (sim + design)
input.head: claude/github-executor-pricing-l3qqot
input.body:
Actions bills each job's runtime rounded **up** to the next minute, so a day's cost is the workflow-run count, not the minutes worked. The queue's shape maximized that count: one-item executor runs chained by self-re-dispatch (a whole invocation of checkout, setup and rounding per item), plus an hourly drain dispatched even into an empty queue — ~48 runs for a quiet day, ~55 for a working one.

The simulator half of #1212, per the sim's change-the-simulator-first discipline (the engine and workflow wiring follow in #1214):

- **`sim.mjs`** — an executor run drains until nothing is pickable, settling items serially in the same run (the occupancy model is unchanged; the dead-run remainder still goes to the failure-continuation job). The scheduler run schedules its drain only when its parting look at the queue found something pickable, and records `drain-skipped` otherwise. The operator hold is re-read between items, so suspension still parks the train at most one item later. `actionExecutions()` accounts every billed workflow run — suspended starts included — by workflow and executor trigger.
- **Scenarios** — new S65 pins a working day (the morning chain, tidy, a release, a marked request, a hand-created manual-task item) at **29 invocations**: the cron's 24 scheduler runs, four drains, one label event — the 04:00 anchor's three items settle in one run. New S66 pins the quiet day at the **24-run cron floor** with zero executor starts. S34/S36 rewritten to the batched-drain invariants (one run settles its hour; a dead run's settled items stand, its run-end is never written). Both regressions — the unconditional drain and one-item runs — were re-introduced deliberately and watched go red on exactly these tests.
- **DESIGN.md** — decision §15.30 records the reversal of §15.22 ("one run performs one item", owner 2026-08-22); §6, §8, §10, §15.17/§15.22/§15.24 amended in place; the executor-run cause list loses self-re-dispatch.
- **SCENARIOS.md / sim README** — section N (S65/S66), the S34/S36/S37 replays, coverage-map rows, and the Actions-variable-delivery boundary row updated to the between-items API re-read.

Full suite: 2522 tests, all green (the shims test needs a full-depth clone, as it says). `check_the_work`/`check_the_world`: 0 blocking, nothing on these files.

Closes #1213

The engine still runs the old shape until #1214 lands, so its files were deliberately not touched.

**The model change** (three pieces, all recorded as DESIGN decision §15.30 in [DESIGN.md](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/github-executor-pricing-l3qqot/docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md)):
- an executor run drains until nothing is pickable, settling items serially in the same run — self-re-dispatch retires; the failure-continuation job still covers a run that dies mid-batch;
- the scheduler's drain job dispatches only when the scheduler run leaves something pickable, so idle hours cost the cron's one run;
- the operator hold is re-read between items (API read — the env copy lands at start only), so suspension still parks the train at most one item later.

**The accounting and the day scenarios** ([sim.mjs](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/github-executor-pricing-l3qqot/docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/sim.mjs), [SCENARIOS.md](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/github-executor-pricing-l3qqot/docs/tasks-dispatch/SCENARIOS.md) §N): `actionExecutions()` counts every billed workflow run, suspended starts included. **S65** runs a full working day — the 02:00/03:00/04:00 morning chain, tidy, a release, a marked ad-hoc request, a hand-created manual-task item — and asserts seven pieces of work cost exactly **29 invocations** (24 cron + 4 drains + 1 label event; the 04:00 anchor's three items settle in one run). **S66** pins the quiet day at the **24-run cron floor**, zero executor starts — versus ~48 under the old shape. I re-introduced both regressions deliberately and watched exactly these tests go red before restoring.

---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it again.
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.
